subject: music
objective: Describe pitch as how high or low a sound is and connect it to how fast a source vibrates; name notes on the treble staff and the piano keyboard (C4 to G5, including middle C and sharps/flats); state the beat values of whole, half, dotted half, quarter, and eighth notes and rests in 4/4 time and build measures that hold exactly four beats; and read a short melody by pitch and rhythm.
sources: Gotham M, et al. Open Music Theory, Version 2. Chapter: Reading Clefs (C. Hamm) (https://pressbooks.nebraska.edu/openmusictheory/chapter/clefs); LibreTexts mirror (https://human.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Music/Music_Theory/Open_Music_Theory_2e_(Gotham_et_al.)/01%3A_Fundamentals/1.03%3A_Reading_Clefs)
Oklahoma Academic Standards for Fine Arts (2023), to be checked by the teacher before any codes are attached (https://legacy.sde.ok.gov/sites/default/files/2023%20OAS%20FA%20FINAL_0.pdf)
misconceptions: Higher sounds are louder sounds (pitch and loudness are the same thing)
Higher on the staff or keyboard does not match higher in sound
Every white key is a whole step from the next (E-F and B-C are half steps)
Black keys have only one name
The musical alphabet goes past G (H, I, ...)
A note's length depends on how high it is, or every note gets one beat
A half note and a whole note are the same because both are hollow
A dot after a note is decoration
A measure can hold any number of beats in 4/4
modelLimitations: Sound is a computer-made tone (Web Audio), not a recorded instrument; it has a simpler timbre than a real piano.
The vibration picture is a simple sine wave; real instruments make complex waves with overtones.
Frequencies assume standard equal-temperament tuning with A4 = 440 Hz and are rounded.
Only the treble clef and 4/4 time are used. Bass clef, other time signatures, key signatures, ties, and sixteenth notes are left out.
Songs are transposed to C and simplified (one line of Twinkle, Twinkle; Ode to Joy as commonly taught to beginners).
The song activity checks note order only, not rhythm or timing.
Ear-training questions use random notes and loudness; nothing is stored.
